transcript: In the 20th century, most vaccines took well over a decade to research, test and produce. But the vaccines for COVID-19 cleared the threshold for emergency use in less than 11 months. The secret behind this speed is a medical technology that's been developing for decades, the mRNA vaccine. This new treatment uses our body's existing cellular machinery to trigger an immune response, protecting us from viruses without ever experiencing an infection. And in the future, this approach might be able to treat new diseases almost as quickly as they emerge. So how do these revolutionary vaccines work? The key ingredient is in the name. mRNA, or messenger ribonucleic acid, is a naturally occurring molecule that encodes the instructions for producing proteins. When our cells process mRNA, a part of the cell, called the ribosome, translates and follows these instructions to build the encoded protein. The mRNA in these vaccines works in exactly the same way, but scientists use the molecule to safely introduce our body to a virus. First, researchers encode trillions of mRNA molecules with the instructions for a specific viral protein. This part of the virus is harmless by itself, but helpful for training our body's immune response. Then, they inject those molecules into a nanoparticle, roughly a thousand times smaller than the average cell. This nanoparticle is made of lipids, the same type of fatty material that forms the membrane around our cells. But these lipids have been specially engineered to protect the mRNA on its journey through the body and assist its entry into the cell. Lastly, the final ingredients are added, sugars and salt, to help keep the nanoparticles intact until they reach their destination. Before use, the vaccine is kept at a temperature of minus 20 to minus 80 degrees Celsius to ensure none of the components break down. Once injected, the nanoparticles disperse and encounter cells. The lipid coating on each nanoparticle fuses with the lipid membrane of a cell and releases the mRNA to do its work. At this point, we should note that while the vaccine is delivering viral genetic material into our cells, it's impossible for this material to alter our DNA. mRNA is a short-lived molecule that would need additional enzymes and chemical signals to even access our DNA, let alone change it. And none of these DNA altering components are present in mRNA vaccines. Once inside the cell, the ribosome translates the mRNA's instructions and begins assembling the viral protein. In COVID-19 vaccines, that protein is one of the spikes typically found on the virus's surface. Without the rest of the virus, this lone spike is not infectious. But it does trigger our immune response. Activating the immune system can be taxing on the body, resulting in brief fatigue, fever and muscle soreness in some people. But this doesn't mean the recipient is sick. It means the vaccine is working. The body is producing antibodies to fight that viral protein that will then stick around to defend against future COVID-19 infections. And since this particular protein is likely to be found in most COVID variants, these antibodies should reduce the threat of catching new strains. This approach offers significant advantages over previous vaccines. Traditional vaccines contain weakened versions of live viruses or amputated sections of a virus, both of which require time-intensive research to prepare and unique chemical treatments to safely inject. But mRNA vaccines don't actually contain any viral particles, so they don't have to be built from scratch to safely adjust each virus. In fact, every mRNA vaccine could have roughly the same list of ingredients. Imagine a reliable, robustly tested vaccine that can treat any disease by swapping out a single component. To treat a new illness, researchers would identify the right viral protein, encode it into mRNA and then swap that mRNA into the existing vaccine platform. This could make it possible to develop new vaccines in weeks, giving humanity a flexible new tool in the never-ending fight against disease. But where did vaccines get started? Watch this video to travel back to 1796, when an 8-year-old boy changed the course of history. Or get the answer to a pressing question. When exactly is a pandemic over?

description:
Do vaccines really contain microchips that can track people?

This video investigates one of the most persistent claims surrounding COVID-19 vaccines — and follows the technology, biology, and evidence behind it.

The short answer: COVID-19 vaccines do not contain microchips or tracking devices. The CDC has specifically addressed this claim, and WHO has identified it as false misinformation.

The bigger question is how a claim like this became so convincing in the first place.

Sources: CDC, World Health Organization

And even if you could shrink the electronics, there's a bigger question. Where would the chip get enough power to track anything or transmit data? And there's another problem. The electronics would have to be incredibly small to pass through a standard vaccine needle, while still containing everything needed to function. And then there's the network problem. A tracking device would need to communicate with external receivers, meaning it needs the right hardware to send and receive signals. So when you look at the engineering, the claim falls apart. A vaccine needle can't secretly deliver a powered, network-connected tracking chip. The evidence simply isn't there.

title: How are mRNA and protein-based COVID-19 vaccines different?
description:
Welcome to Immunize.org’s Ask the Experts resources. This Ask the Experts question is presented by Immunize.org’s Kelly L. Moore, MD, MPH. 

Question: 
How are mRNA and protein-based COVID-19 vaccines different?

Answer: 
All vaccines work by triggering an immune response inside our bodies. This immune response, which produces antibodies, helps protect us from illness caused by the pathogen targeted by those antibodies and other elements of the immune system. COVID-19 vaccines all train the immune system to recognize parts of the spike protein found on the surface of the SARS-CoV-2 virus, but they do so in different ways. 

The messenger RNA (or mRNA) vaccines, including the Pfizer-BioNTech COVID-19 Vaccine (Comirnaty) and the Moderna COVID-19 vaccines (Spikevax and mNexspike) are lipid nanoparticle-formulated, nucleoside-modified mRNA vaccines that encode the prefusion spike glycoprotein of the virus that causes COVID-19. To speak simply, these vaccines contain a messenger RNA recipe for a harmless piece of the spike protein found on the surface of SARS-CoV-2. The messenger RNA is enclosed in fatty bubbles that enable it to enter our cells where our own cellular machinery temporarily makes the spike protein pieces from the mRNA before that mRNA is broken down and discarded from the body. Messenger RNA is not able to enter the nucleus of the cell where our genes are located and, therefore, it does not alter our genes. 

The adjuvanted protein subunit COVID-19 vaccine developed by Novavax and commercialized by Sanofi is called Nuvaxovid. It’s a traditional vaccine that contains the pre-made spike protein that the immune system needs to be trained to recognize. It also contains an adjuvant called “Matrix-M” that is added to enhance the immune response to the vaccine. The saponin-based adjuvant is made from extracts of the bark of the Soapbark tree native to Chile. The spike protein in Nuvaxovid is produced in insect cells. 

Although these vaccines work in different ways, they achieve same end result—training the immune system to recognize and respond effectively to the SARS-CoV-2 virus when it infects the body, reducing the vaccinated person’s risk of serious COVID-19 disease. 

About Ask the Experts 
Immunize.org established Ask the Experts to provide practical answers to clinical questions about vaccines and vaccine administration. Our Immunize.org experts have answered more than 1,200 clinical questions like this one based on ACIP recommendations. You can find all of these questions and answers on our "Ask the Experts" page at http://www.immunize.org/askexperts.

We work to improve national and state vaccine policy. Immunize.org also facilitates communication about the safety, efficacy, and use of vaccines within the broad immunization community of patients, parents, healthcare organizations, and government health agencies.

Scientists have long believed that animal viruses need time to evolve before they can efficiently infect humans, but new research suggests some viruses may already carry the biological “key” they need from the moment they appear.

This video examines discoveries involving SARS-CoV-2, bat coronaviruses found in Laos, MERS, the 1918 Spanish Flu, and new research into how viruses cross the species barrier. When researchers used genomic sequencing techniques to map out the MERS-CoV viruses found in both humans and camels, they discovered a disturbing fact. The two are almost exactly the same. To be more precise, they are 99.9% identical. They are not distant relatives but biological mirror images. That means that this virus doesn't need any sort of learning or adaptation period to bridge the gap from one species to another. There isn't some vast chasm separating the two, but a tiny almost imperceptible 0.1% gap. The virus can simply cross the species barrier using the exact same architecture it relies on to infect livestock and other animal populations. It is a fully functional, completely compatible and capable invader, a microscopic weapon of mass destruction that is more adaptable than we ever thought possible. The implications of this are terrifying from a biosecurity standpoint. This discovery suggests that virologists might have been working on flawed information for years. They have been looking for the wrong warning signs, following unreliable models, and allowing society to sleepwalk its way toward another biological crisis. If animal-based viruses like MERS-CoV are already identical to the human killing versions, then how many more of them are out there just waiting to kick off the next pandemic? By the early 2020s, we knew that there were viruses out there that could move from animals to humans far faster than anticipated. Scientists had proved this was the case with the likes of the Spanish flu and MERS-CoV, but they still were seen by many as outliers or anomalies. Then a groundbreaking 2024 study arrived. It showed that these alleged anomalies might be a part of a larger and deeply worrying trend. The study was carried out by researchers at the Bloom Lab at the Fred Hutch Cancer Center, led by evolutionary biologist Jesse Bloom. It was designed to put the evolutionary barrier hypothesis to the ultimate test. They wanted to know whether viruses actually need time to adapt when they jump into humans, or whether they might already be capable of doing it from the start. To do this, the team didn't just focus on a single outbreak or viral strain. Instead, they analyzed large genomic data sets to understand how they behave at a molecular level. They used a technique called deep mutational scanning to study specific viral proteins in detail. Their analysis covered a wide range of viruses, including influenza, SARS-CoV-2, HIV, and Zika. This allowed them to map out how thousands of potential mutations might affect a virus's ability to evade antibodies and infect cells. First, the researchers had to create a so-called pseudovirus. These were safe versions of real pathogens that were able to enter cells but unable to replicate. This eliminated the multiple risks associated with working with live dangerous viral strains. They were then able to genetically engineer the viral proteins to make their own mutations. It was similar to the ways a viral cell might change or adapt to increase its infectivity and ability to survive in different hosts and environments. The variants were then tested and researchers measured how well they resisted antibodies and how tightly they attached themselves to the host cells. The data pointed in one direction. Some of the deadliest pandemics in human history had zero adaptation time during their initial outbreaks. In other words, when these strains first entered the human population, they didn't immediately need to evolve to become more effective at infecting us or evading the immune system.
